"It was ferocious… I saw the fire jump [from one building to another] - then a huge fireball burst. It was truly hell on Earth. How could anyone possibly escape?" said Mrs Lau.
She tried calling her husband again. This time, there was no answer.
The body of Lau Man Kwong was eventually found by rescuers - he had locked himself inside the toilet.
"He was wearing his slippers, sitting on the toilet and clutching his identity card," said his wife, who added that she escaped death "by the narrowest margin".
"I would have held onto my husband and died with him.
"He was such a good person. I just don't understand why he had to die in such a terrible way."
Mr Lau and his wife moved into Wang Fuk Court in 1983 - the year the building was completed.
She recalls an idyllic life - a family with three children who were able to grow up close to the sea and spend weekends playing at a nearby park.
"All three of my children adored my husband… He could be very stern, and I was the only woman who could make him laugh."
No way out
In 2024, mandated renovations began in Wang Fuk Court.
In Hong Kong, all buildings over 30 years old have to undergo an inspection - and any necessary renovations as a result.

Like many building complexes in Hong Kong, Wang Fuk Court had a management committee that oversaw things like building repairs. As many as 57 construction companies submitted bids. But the company that won, Prestige Construction and Engineering (PC&E), submitted the most expensive bid at HK$336m ($42.8m; £32.4m).

Residents, many of whom were over 65, had to bear the cost. The hefty bills triggered protests but eventually, the contract was signed. But once the renovations began in July 2024, residents were unhappy.
Among the complaints was that workers constantly smoked on site, dropping cigarette butts everywhere.
The 1,154 page report suggested the fire was caused by a lit cigarette.
Figure caption,
Watch: Christy says she still sends WhatsApp messages to her husband who died in the blaze

There were also complaints about most of Wang Fuk Court's eight buildings having their windows taped over with foam boards to stop debris falling in - blocking daylight or any sort of view at all, for months.
All eight buildings were also covered in a protective mesh netting and bamboo scaffolding.

The report also found that after typhoons damaged the original scaffolding nets in 2025, cheaper non-fire-retardant replacements were chosen - something that was done as a "cost-saving measure at the expense of the safety of the residents".

Residents had filed nearly 140 complaints to six government departments, including the fire services and the buildings departments, in and after 2024, but these were largely ignored, the report went on to say.
It also revealed that a staff member of the estate's property manager, ISS, had turned off the power supply to the fire alarms in all eight buildings - which is why no alarms rang on the day itself.
ISS later told the BBC it had "reviewed and reinforced its procedures [and] staff training" in Hong Kong, adding that it takes the findings of the report "very seriously".

But for those who did manage to flee their homes - the emergency staircase turned out to be another death trap. Windows were removed from some fire escape stairwells to create temporary openings for workers - letting in smoke and cutting off vital escape routes.
Dozens, including Christy's husband, died in such stairwells.

blocks.alt: On the right there is a bespectacled woman looks far into the distance while holding a boy. A young girl stands besides them. Only the backs of the children can be seen.

blocks.text: Image source, Lam Yik / BBC Chinese
Image caption,
Christy's daughter celebrated her ninth birthday the day before the fire

Christy, who wanted to be identified only by her first name, says her husband was at home alone when the fire broke out. She only found out about it when her friends sent her messages about it. By the time she made it to the apartment complex, it was already cordoned off.
She found out later that he had died of smoke inhalation in the stairwell, something she says that is at least of some consolation to her.
"My husband's body would have been burnt and he would have been in more pain if he was at home. At the very least… his suffering was minimal."
Christy says her family had just celebrated their eldest child's ninth birthday the day before - they had saved some leftover cake in the fridge to eat the next day. Their father never got to eat it.
Both children have been deeply affected by the loss of their father.
Her youngest child, a seven-year-old boy, had "covered his ears and yelled" when he was first told what had happened to his father.
He now often comforts his mother, saying he will take care of her as he is the only man in the family.
"He hides his emotions. A seven-year-old child should not behave this way, and I feel heartbroken," says Christy, who has herself been diagnosed with PTSD and depression.
Her daughter has "extreme thoughts" she says, and channels her emotions through art.
She turned 10 on Wednesday, but this year, there was no birthday celebration in sight.
Her birthday, she says, will now instead be a day to commemorate her father.
Bid-rigging and rubber stamps
Wang Fuk Court's problems date back to before the renovations began.

The management company hired to oversee and supervise the project, Will Power, conspired with PC&E to defraud residents in Wang Fuk Court, according to the city's Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC).

Although PC&E was found to have breached safety requirements and violated building department rules for multiple previous projects, homeowners at Wang Fuk Court were told that they had a clean record.

The ICAC alleges that this was part of a lucrative scheme, with Will Power's director Wong Hap-yin, along with other individuals, laundering over $5m in suspected proceeds from the tendering process from Wang Fuk Court, among other housing projects.

Once PC&E cinched the contract, Will Power's registered inspector - an individual meant to oversee the renovations - merely rubber-stamped the documents, without having actually conducted any inspections personally, the report added.
Will Power has been since liquidated and PC&E could not be reached for a response.

Both companies - Will Power and PC&E - and seven individuals have been charged with 25 counts of offences including including manslaughter, conspiracy to defraud, attempting to pervert the course of public justice and tax evasion.
Four of them are still in custody but none of the cases have gone to trial yet.
The report said both companies involved were the "main culprits responsible".

But it also directed heavy criticism at authorities, saying that "no government department took effective ownership of various fire safety issues and complaints about fire hazards fell into a vacuum".

One expert, Prof John Burns of Hong Kong University, had called the event the "largest governance crisis" that authorities have faced since 2020 - a reference to the controversial National Security Law that was passed in that year.

On the day the report was released, almost one year after the fire, Hong Kong's housing chief Winnie Ho resigned and the city's top leader John Lee apologised for the first time, promising that a "large number" of reforms would be rolled out.

blocks.alt: Thick smoke and flames rise as a major fire engulfs several apartment blocks at Wang Fuk Court

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Homeowners at Wang Fuk Court (pictured) were told their construction company had a clean record
A shell of a home
Five months after the fire, Mrs Lau was allowed into her flat for the first time to collect any personal belongings that might have remained.
In her first visit, she was given just three hours to retrieve 40 years' worth of belongings.
Pictures taken from the visit show a home that has been utterly burned out - with every surface blackened and soot covering the floor.
"I almost fainted when I saw what had become of my home. I don't understand how the home I had built, such a warm and beautiful home, could end up like this," said Mrs Lau.

blocks.alt: The metal frame of a wheelchair stands in a flat strewn with ashes

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied
Image caption,
The frame of Mr Lau's wheelchair was one of the few things left in their burnt home

Her children, who came with her, described the house as a "war zone". Among the rubble, they found broken pieces of a piggy bank that Mr Lau had dutifully filled with coins every day for the past 20 years.
"Everyone in our family knew it was his favourite possession. The piggy bank died with him," said Mrs Lau.
Mrs Lau and her daughter have since rented a place nearby to live - and she is worried about how she is going to afford a new house.
The government has said it will spend $867m (£663m) to acquire affected flats - but Mrs Lau says it is not nearly enough to buy a similarly sized flat in the area.
Still, her family was in a better position than many others, she said.
"Should I say that we are fortunate?
"I lost my husband but many families lost multiple family members... Babies less than a year old died. "
Stories have emerged of some of the other victims - a six-month-old who died alongside her 68-year-old grandmother when the fire broke out.
The bodies of an Indonesian domestic helper and the elderly person she worked for were found huddled together.

blocks.alt: Mrs Lau, in a pink shirt, holds a piggy bank. There are two more piggy banks on the shelf

blocks.text: Image source, BBC Chinese / Phoebe Kong
Image caption,
Mrs Lau's son has since bought new piggy banks in memory of his father
As for Christy, she says she is planning to file a lawsuit against those responsible for the fire - but acknowledges that even if she wins, she "can't [get] my husband's life back".
"I share things that happen in our daily life, as if he still existed," she says. "I often write to him, 'I miss you so much. Are you doing well on the other side?'"
It's a similar story for Mrs Lau, who says she can't go anywhere without seeing her husband.
"Every day, something reminds me of him," she said.
"I still find it very hard to accept that my husband is gone, my home is gone, and so many of my neighbours are gone…. This place was my roots. I never imagined it would also mark an ending for me."

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported nine measles-related deaths in the United States this year, as the country battles its worst outbreak of the highly contagious viral infection in decades.

The US had recorded 6,039 confirmed measles cases as of Nov 24, across 47 jurisdictions, according to the agency's website on Wednesday. That includes 18 cases among international visitors.

The CDC updated its tally after the National Center for Health Statistics received additional reports from states and verified that the deaths had occurred and that measles was the underlying cause, a Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson said.

Based on publicly reported state figures, however, the US has recorded at least 14 measles-associated deaths this year, including nine fatalities in Pennsylvania, three in Wisconsin and one each in Virginia and New York state.

A discrepancy between state and federal death tallies arose earlier this year after CDC, under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., began using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data instead of state figures.

"The discrepancy between state and federal measles-related death figures is concerning and risks confusing the public about the true toll of this outbreak," said Frederic Bertley, immunologist and CEO of the Center of Science and Industry.

"Regardless of the precise number, these deaths are alarming and reflect the consequences of declining vaccination coverage," Bertley said.

Cases in the US have reached a 35-year high, a resurgence driven largely by unvaccinated people that this month stripped the country of its hard-fought measles elimination status.

CDC data showed that 671 patients, or 11 per cent of confirmed cases, were hospitalised, with children aged under 5 years recording the highest hospitalisation rate at 17 per cent. The agency also said the death count could change as it reviews additional information.

On Wednesday, Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit US state, reported 1,679 measles cases so far this year, including 87 new cases over the past seven days and 340 hospitalisations.

Andy Taylor, guitarist of new wave icons Duran Duran, dies at 65

Taylor revealed during Duran Duran’s November 2022 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction that he had stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.

The original members of British pop group Duran Duran, from left to right, Andy Taylor, John Taylor, Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes and Roger Taylor pose for pictures at a news conference in Hong Kong on Aug 26, 2004. (AP Photo/Lo Sai-hung, File)

FAST

Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of the 1980s English new wave band Duran Duran, whose huge pop hits include Hungry Like the Wolf, The Reflex and Rio and whose rise up the charts was inextricably linked to the launch of MTV, has died. He was 65.

Taylor's death was confirmed by his family and bandmates in a statement posted on social media and Duran Duran's website.

“From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed,” the band said.

On the night he was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in November 2022, Taylor revealed that he had been battling stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer for several years and was unable to attend.

“I would like to thank each of my brothers in this great band,” he wrote. “You can dream about what happened to us but to experience it, on one’s own terms, as mates, was beyond incredible.”

The two-time Grammy Award winners had nine gold records and six platinum ones, with 20 Top 20 singles in the UK and 18 in the US. They were two-time Ivor Novello Award winners and are MTV Video Visionary Award recipients.

The band’s imperial stage occurred with a trio of hit albums between 1981 and 1983, with such dance-floor barnburners as Girls On Film and Union Of The Snake and the moody ballads The Chauffeur and Save A Prayer. Other hits in the coming years included The Wild Boys, New Moon On Monday and Come Undone. Their popularity was cemented when they recorded the James Bond theme song A View To A Kill and earned a slot at Live Aid in 1985.

Mixing fashion, pioneering synthesisers and glam-pop swagger, the telegenic band were all over radio and young people’s walls, with bassist John Taylor and singer Simon Le Bon becoming heartthrobs and the band being labelled part of the New Romantics. Princess Diana was known to be a fan and that meant a lot to the band.

items.title: Thirty-one killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway
items.summary: Another 21 are injured after the tanker reportedly overturns on a busy ring road in the Egyptian capital.
items.body:
Figure caption,

Huge fire erupts near Cairo killing at least 30 people

ByAleks Phillips

At least 30 people have been killed and 19 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health ministry says.

Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering burns and smoke inhalation after the incident, which occurred on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, to the north of the old city centre, on Wednesday evening.

Unverified footage circulating on social media showed billowing flames and black smoke towering high into the night sky, with multiple nearby vehicles torched.

Officials have not given an account of how the fire broke out, but state-owned media reported the tanker had overturned, dousing nearby vehicles with petrol.

The regional public prosecutor has launched an investigation into the incident and asked that DNA samples be taken from bodies of the dead.

The tanker, which belonged to a private contractor, had been travelling along the highway when a high-voltage cable fell in front of it, prompting the driver to lose control, Al-Ahram reports, citing sources with knowledge of the investigation.

It then crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire, the state-owned newspaper says.

Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years, with informal residential areas and often run-down infrastructure making incidents more common, the response to which is often complicated by slow emergency response times and locally improvised rescue efforts, even in the sprawling Egyptian capital.

Images from the scene show a large crowd gathered on the highway after the fire had been extinguished, as emergency services blocked off entry routes.

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Images from the scene show a large crowd gathered on the highway after the fire had been extinguished

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

The tanker crossed the highway's central reservation before overturning and bursting into flames, local media report

The health ministry said 39 ambulances had been dispatched to respond to the fire, while it posted images of Egypt's health minister overseeing the treatment of the injured at one of Cairo's hospitals.

Road collisions are also common in Egypt, often attributed to lax maintenance and the widespread flouting of traffic laws.

Nearly 6,000 people died on Egypt's roads last year, official figures show, a rise of several hundred on the previous year's total.

Emergency responders have since cleared the highway and allowed it to reopen, state broadcaster NMA reports.

A bulldozer could earlier be seen at the scene clearing the burnt-out wrecks of cars.

items.title: Commentary: From solving to ‘digesting’: How mathematicians can adapt to the dramatic changes of AI
items.summary: If AI can generate papers that would take a human mathematician years to research and write, does that mean mathematics is dead? A professor gives his take.

Commentary

Commentary: From solving to ‘digesting’: How mathematicians can adapt to the dramatic changes of AI

If AI can generate papers that would take a human mathematician years to research and write, does that mean mathematics is dead? A professor gives his take.

On Nov 20, 2026, a mathematician at the AI company Anthropic claimed that while working with the model Claude, he had solved the generalised Riemann hypothesis, the most famous problem in mathematics. (Photo: iStock/PhonlamaiPhoto)

David Manderscheid

FAST

KNOXVILLE, Tennessee: Mathematics is having an existential crisis.

On Nov 20, 2026, a mathematician at the AI company Anthropic claimed that while working with the model Claude, he had solved the generalised Riemann hypothesis, the most famous problem in mathematics. This problem has stood unsolved for 167 years, and solving it could easily warrant a Fields Medal – considered equivalent to a Nobel Prize, but for mathematics. In its current state, however, the solution is roughly 250,000 pages long, so it will take a while before human mathematicians can be satisfied that it is correct.

This proof emerged a month after OpenAI released 722 mathematics research papers that contained results generated by an internal AI model. While they have already retracted some of the papers due to mistakes, others, assuming they are correct, would also be impressive enough to earn a Fields Medal.

If AI can generate papers that would take a human mathematician years to research and write, does that mean mathematics is dead? Many headlines have been asking this question – and some school-age children may be rejoicing.

But it’s not that simple. I’ve been a mathematician for 45 years, and my work has taught me that mathematics is not just about solving problems or proving theorems. It is about understanding why the solutions and proofs work and then extending that mathematics to new contexts.

Fueling this existential crisis is the fact that over the past century, mathematicians have come to attach greater prestige to the solution and the proof than the understanding. Now that an AI can come up with a solution and a proof, the underlying understanding could vanish. Mathematicians are being forced to rethink what they value.

WHY SHOULD NONMATHEMATICIANS CARE?

If you’re not a mathematician, this crisis might seem inconsequential. But math isn’t all abstract problems. It’s used to design and optimise technology that’s essential to modern society.

One example is MRI, or magnetic resonance imaging. MRI is a very useful tool in medical diagnosis. X-rays see only your bones, but MRI machines allow a physician to see the soft tissue inside a person in a noninvasive manner.

MRI scans used to require a patient to lie still inside a metal tube for up to half an hour or more while a loud machine made images by scanning back and forth. At the end, it combined the images. This process was difficult for many adults and virtually impossible for children without sedation.

Commentary: The human advantage in the age of AI

Commentary: This is the problem with the circular AI economy

Modern MRI machines require many fewer scans in a shorter period, and they get better resolution. Now, more patients find the procedure no big deal. The key to this vast improvement was the mathematics of compressed sensing, a relatively recent invention.

Compressed sensing allows the machine to construct an image from fewer scans. At first, doing so didn’t seem possible. But in the mid 2000s, a mathematician, statisticians and an electrical engineer figured out how to use the fact that many of the scans are very similar to develop the mathematics that made compressed sensing possible.

They showed that images can be reconstructed from far fewer samples than previously thought necessary. This solution required a deep understanding of many different areas of mathematics, and even the development of new mathematics. items.title: North Korea expels Swiss diplomat in sanctions row
items.summary: Swiss officials said relations would be kept through North Korea's embassy in Bern, and its own embassy in Beijing.
items.body:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang

ByPaul Gribben

North Korea has ordered Switzerland's diplomatic representative to leave the country within 48 hours and called for the office to close amid a row over sanctions.

It said the move was in response to Switzerland's decision to place sanctions on the Songdowon international children's camp. State media described this as "a blatant hostile act".

That camp is at the centre of claims that it was involved in transferring children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.

North Korea's foreign ministry said "any act of violating the sovereign rights" of the country and the interests of its citizens "can never be welcomed".

Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang.

Swiss authorities said relations between the two countries would be maintained through the North Korean embassy in Bern, and the Swiss embassy in Beijing.

The diplomatic rebuke comes weeks after Swiss foreign minister Ignazio Cassis made a rare visit to North Korea, where he officially reopened the office and discussed normalising relations.

Diplomatic links with North Korea were first established in 1974 and Switzerland opened a co-operation office in Pyongyang in 1997.

Image source, KCNA via AP

Image caption,

A Swiss delegation, on left, including Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis, met with North Korean officials in Pyongyang last month

Switzerland's federal department of foreign affairs said the country "distinguishes between its sanctions policy and its commitment to maintaining dialogue with all countries".

It added: "The reopening of the office in Pyongyang did not in any way affect Switzerland's implementation of UN sanctions related to North Korea's nuclear programme, nor its implementation of EU sanctions targeting North Korea in the context of Russia's war against Ukraine."

Thousands of North Korean soldiers have been deployed to help support Russia's war with Ukraine.

In August, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Moscow of using North Korean missiles.

Israeli judges recommend prosecutors drop one bribery case against Netanyahu

Israeli judges have recommended dropping one of three corruption cases against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and reconsidering another, in a trial that began in 2020.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu arrives to speak to the media at the Knesset, Israel's parliament in Jerusalem, Nov 25, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/Ronen Zvulun)

JERUSALEM: Israeli judges on Wednesday (Nov 25) recommended that prosecutors drop one of three long-running cases against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and reconsider another alleging he granted favours in exchange for positive media coverage.

Netanyahu was indicted in 2019 on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust. He denies the charges and has pleaded not guilty. His trial began in 2020 and involves three criminal cases.

In the case referred to as Case 4000, prosecutors allege that Netanyahu granted regulatory favours worth around 1.8 billion shekels (about US$500 million) to Bezeq Telecom Israel. In return, prosecutors say, he sought positive coverage for himself and his wife, Sara, on a news website controlled by former Bezeq Chairman Shaul Elovitch. Elovitch has denied wrongdoing.

In a blow to prosecutors, Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman of Jerusalem District Court, who presides over Case 4000, told Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara at a hearing on Wednesday that a conviction was unlikely and the case should be dropped.

The recommendation was not a ruling on the case, the court clarified, and Baharav-Miara said she would review the court's statements with the prosecution.

The judges also recommended prosecutors reconsider so-called Case 2000 because of doubts that Netanyahu's actions constituted a criminal offence. In that case, prosecutors allege Netanyahu negotiated a deal with Arnon Mozes, owner of Israel's Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper, for better coverage in return for legislation to slow the growth of a rival newspaper.

Netanyahu on Wednesday called the court's recommendation a "ray of light for truth and justice."

"Ten years of suffering for dozens of my close ones who were dragged into interrogation rooms," Netanyahu said in a televised address. "Where they were blackmailed with criminal acts, humiliated, and the lives of many of them were ruined, just so they would give false testimony against me."

'Russia wants more than Ukraine,' says Germany's Merz as he defends aid for Kyiv

BERLIN: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz accused Russia on Wednesday (Nov 25) of "escalating" threats to European security as he defended his government's plans to bolster defence spending and maintain financial aid to Ukraine.

Opposition parties, including the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which tops national opinion polls, and the hard-left Die Linke, have called for an end to military aid to Kyiv.

"It cannot be said often enough, against the far right as much as the far left: Russia knows exactly what it wants. And Russia wants more than Ukraine," Merz told the Bundestag lower house of parliament during a debate on the 2027 draft budget.

"Russia is escalating in the Baltic region, in Poland, on the Black Sea; Russia is escalating in space, and Russia is by now also escalating massively here in our own country," he said.

Russia did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment on Merz's accusations. It has repeatedly denied seeking military confrontation with NATO countries and says its actions in Ukraine are aimed at protecting its own national security.

Merz's government blamed Russia in September for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport, an accusation the Russian Embassy in Berlin dismissed as part of a "new wave of anti-Russian hysteria in Germany".

Germany and other European countries have also been hit by a wave of cyberattacks and sabotage incidents targeting critical infrastructure that they have often blamed on Russia. Moscow has denied all the allegations.

"LEARNING FROM UKRAINE"

Merz said on Wednesday that by supporting Ukraine, Germany was also protecting itself.

"We are learning from Ukraine - technologically for civilian use but of course also in defence technology," he said.

Germany has been Ukraine's biggest military backer in Europe since Russia's full-blown invasion on Feb 24, 2022, but public support for this policy has decreased amid cost-of-living pressures. A poll published on Tuesday showed a narrow majority of Germans now oppose giving military aid to Kyiv.

"Whose chancellor are you, actually?" AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla asked Merz during Wednesday's debate, accusing the government of supporting Ukraine while failing to provide sufficient relief to German citizens. "What a mockery!"

Germany aims to double defence spending to over €200 billion (US$228 billion) between now and 2030, according to the 2027 draft budget, hitting 3.7 per cent of national output by 2030, in line with commitments to NATO.

EU SHOULD FOCUS ON SECURITY AND COMPETITIVENESS, MERZ SAYS

Merz also addressed on Wednesday the latest proposal for the European Union budget for 2028-2034 presented by European Council chief Antonio Costa.

Costa proposed cuts that would reduce the overall seven-year ⁠budget to €1.582 trillion, some €40 billion less than a proposal presented by the ​Irish EU presidency in October.

EU leaders will discuss Costa's proposals at a special summit ‌on Thursday and Friday.

"In these negotiations I am pushing for spending to be limited and focused on what really makes Europe stronger: security and competitiveness," Merz said. "If spending is focused, it is the best additional insurance for our country."

Moment Nasa spacecraft hit asteroid - and what happened next

The first images of an asteroid that Nasa deliberately crashed into have revealed a stadium-sized crater on its surface.

Video released by Nasa showed the moment of impact in 2022, while new images show the extent of the damage done to the asteroid.

Dimorphos, the asteroid, posed no threat to Earth, but the crash was a test of our planetary defences to see if it was possible to knock a space rock off course.

Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision.

LONDON: The Saudi sovereign wealth fund is seeking to sell up to 25 per cent of Newcastle in order to fund major infrastructure investments at the Premier League club, the Athletic reported on Wednesday (Nov 25).

A 2021 takeover led by the Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF) has not had the transformative effect on the Magpies' fortunes that many fans dreamed of.

The club won the League Cup - their first domestic trophy for 70 years - in 2025, and twice secured qualification for the Champions League.

But they have been hampered by financial sustainability rules while recent cutbacks, including the withdrawal of funding for LIV Golf, suggest a change in strategy by the PIF.

The British Reuben family owns around 16 per cent of Newcastle, with the remaining shares held by the PIF.

The Athletic reported that fresh investment would be used to help fund an upgraded training facility and stadium redevelopment.

items.title: Peter Magyar meets Volodymyr Zelenskyy: Hungary and Ukraine make a fresh start after the icy relations of the Viktor Orban era
items.summary: After years of frosty and hostile relations under Hungary's Kremlin-friendly former PM Viktor Orban, his successor, Peter Magyar, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy seek to reset their countries' ties.
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5PtkN

Prefer DW on Google

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar (left, pictured here with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy) said his visit to Ukraine marked the beginning of a new chapter in the relationship between Kyiv and BudapestImage: Genya Savilov/AFP

Advertisement

The location and the gesture were carefully chosen: Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stood side by side, laid flowers and bowed their heads at the military cemetery in the center of the Ukrainian city of Uzhhorod.

One of those buried there is an ethnic Hungarian who was one of the first soldiers killed in Russia's full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine.

Magyar intentionally chose not to begin his first visit to Ukraine as prime minister at a government building. Instead, his Tuesday afternoon visit began at a place where he could demonstrate his solidarity with Ukraine more clearly than anywhere else.

Uzhhorod, known as Ungvar in Hungarian, is the capital of Ukraine's Transcarpathia region, which is home to around 80,000 members of Ukraine's Hungarian minority. Thousands of ethnic Hungarians are fighting Russian occupying forces on the front lines.

For Hungary, where ethnic Hungarian minorities in neighboring countries traditionally play an important role, the war is therefore closer to home than it is for other European countries.

Magyar described his visit to Ukraine as a "historic day" in a Facebook post. Before the ceremony at the cemetery in Uzhhorod, he said: "I bring with me the solidarity of the Hungarian people. We stand with Ukraine against the Russian aggressor."

Zelenskyy responded on X, saying "We appreciate this gesture of respect toward those who sacrificed their lives for Ukraine's independence."

From low point to fresh start

The meeting between Magyar and Zelenskyy marked a turning point in Hungary's approach to Ukraine.

The two leaders repeatedly shook hands throughout the day. Such scenes would have been unthinkable just a few months ago. The propaganda of Magyar's pro-Russian predecessor, Viktor Orban, portrayed Ukraine as a "mafia state" and "lawless country" on an almost daily basis.

Under Orban, relations between Hungary and Ukraine reached a historic low.

Now the two countries are seeking a political reset, which is important not only for Hungary and Ukraine but for Europe as a whole. After all, Orban's repeated obstruction of support for Ukraine drove the EU to the brink of despair.

Closer economic cooperation

During talks in Uzhhorod, the two leaders also agreed to closer economic cooperation.

Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar (left) and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy laid wreaths and flowers at a ceremony commemorating the Ukrainian defenders who fell during the Russian invasionImage: Janos Nemes/MTI/AP Photo/picture alliance

The talks centered on Hungarian diesel supplies to Ukraine, greater use of Ukrainian gas storage facilities by Hungarian companies, and joint infrastructure projects, including the opening of new border crossings and a direct rail link between Budapest and Kyiv.

Nevertheless, no formal agreements were signed on Tuesday.

At a subsequent news conference, journalists asked questions about sensitive issues between the two countries: minority rights, Ukraine's EU integration and a new EU loan for Ukraine.

Throughout the day, the two men were visibly keen to avoid any discord.

Magyar, for example, described his angry outburst over Ukraine's "Carpathian Eight" initiative in parliament in late September as a "misunderstanding" and suggested that Hungary might, after all, take part.

Zelenskyy's cautious replies to journalists suggest that he knows his country's path to EU membership also runs through Budapest.

A fresh — but not always smooth — start

One of Magyar's statements on Tuesday was key: "We've finally put a stop to this completely unnecessary and inexplicable political escalation."

Even before taking office in early May 2026, Magyar had promised to reset relations with Ukraine. But the process has not been entirely smooth.

Posters belonging to Viktor Orban's Fidesz party portrayed Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Peter Magyar and Ursula von der Leyen as a risk and Fidesz as 'the better choice' in the run-up to the parliamentary election in AprilImage: Martin Fejer/estost.net/EST&OST/IMAGO

In many respects — but certainly not all — Magyar is distancing himself from his predecessor. He has made no bones of the fact that he sees Russia as the aggressor, but he rejects both arms deliveries to Ukraine and even the transit of weapons across Hungarian territory.

Magyar previously accused Ukraine of treating ethnic Hungarians as second-class citizens — a claim that is not borne out by the facts. He pressed for greater minority rights and for a time blocked the opening of negotiating chapters in Ukraine's EU accession talks.

Magyar also departed from diplomatic convention by choosing the location of his meeting with Zelenskyy in Ukraine: Indeed, it was Magyar who invited Zelenskyy to Transcarpathia.

Hungarian attitudes to Ukraine

Magyar's sometimes confrontational tone toward Ukraine can also be explained by the need to avoid appearing too pro-Ukrainian to the Hungarian public.

According to a November 2026 poll conducted by the think tank Globsec, 33% of Hungarians would now support their country providing military aid to Ukraine. Although this is much more than during Orban's time in office, many Hungarians remain skeptical of Ukraine.

That's why Olena Halushka, a Ukrainian political scientist at the International Centre for Ukrainian Victory (ICUV), sees some aspects of Magyar's visit as a concession to public opinion in Hungary.

A monument to members of the military killed during Russia's war in Ukraine in the city of Berehove, the political and cultural center of Ukraine's Hungarian minorityImage: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW

"Magyar has taken over a deeply polarized country," she told DW's Ukrainian Service. "A visit to Transcarpathia is more of a step for the Hungarian population than for Ukraine."

Ukraine accommodated not only Magyar's choice of location but also Hungary's demands for better protection of minority rights, which were set out in a 10-point plan in June. That's because EU integration is one of the country's top political priorities.

After planned restrictions on the use of minority languages were withdrawn in late 2023, Ukraine's parliament in early October passed a law on minority language rights that in some respects goes even further than European standards.

Hungary subsequently dropped its obstruction of the opening of negotiating clusters for Ukraine's EU accession.

'Historic' meeting

Laszlo Zubanics, chairman of the Hungarian Democratic Federation in Ukraine (UMDSZ, one of two Hungarian political parties in Transcarpathia), told DW that the Magyar-Zelenskyy meeting was "historic."

He particularly welcomed the fact that Ukraine will probably implement practical improvements in the protection of minority rights "not only by the end of 2027, but much sooner, within just a few months."

Laszlo Zubanics welcomed the fact that Ukraine is likely to implement practical improvements in the protection of minority rights 'within just a few months'Image: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW

A Hungarian diplomat who spoke to DW on condition of anonymity also called the meeting "historic," adding that after the Orban government's anti-Ukrainian policies, trust now needs to be rebuilt, and that personal meetings between the two leaders play an important role in that process.

The diplomat went on to say that Hungary not only wants to ensure that the rights of the Hungarian minority are protected, it also has a strong interest in being involved in Ukraine's reconstruction.

Overall, the diplomat concluded, both sides are very keen to expand economic cooperation.

A path forward

Hungarian political scientist Daniel Hegedus of the Institute for European Politics (IEP) in Berlin told DW that while the meeting was a "symbolic milestone," it will be important to see "how the two political leaders capitalize on the symbolic political capital generated by this meeting."

No observers have suggested that this is the grand finale of reconciliation between Hungary and Ukraine.

Nevertheless, Tuesday's reset sends an important signal to Europe, namely that if the political will is there, a deep gulf that has existed for years can be transformed into a set of diverging interests that can be addressed through negotiations.

Or, as Zelenskyy put it, now there are "all the opportunities to build hopefully constructive relations."

items.title: US Army detonates toxic explosives in Iowa despite contamination fears
items.summary: Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the operation was "a huge success".
items.body:

World

US Army detonates toxic explosives in Iowa despite contamination fears

Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the operation was "a huge success".

The US Army detonates a degraded stockpile of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, US, Nov 25, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/Jim Urquhart)

Read a summary of this article on FAST.

Tap here to return to FAST

FAST

WASHINGTON: The US Army detonated a massive cache of toxic explosives stored in a tiny Iowa farming town Wednesday (Nov 25), saying the materials were too unstable to move to a safer area and warning residents to shelter from the blast and a potential cloud of lead dust.

Officials said the 68 drums of lead azide - the entire US stockpile of the degraded material - were at risk of spontaneous explosion, requiring their destruction at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, where they had been stored for more than 15 years.

Measures were put in place to curb potential contamination from the destruction of the nearly five tons of explosive material, but the Army encouraged residents of Middletown, Iowa and other nearby areas to leave prior to the blast "out of an abundance of caution".

The controlled explosion sent debris flying into the air and a large cloud of smoke over a tree line, while a New York Times reporter said the blast could be heard some 10 miles (15km) away.

US President Donald Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform that "early reports from Iowa are that the Army's mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations".

US Army Acting Secretary Adam Telle speaks at a press conference with other representatives from the military and federal government in Middletown, Iowa, US, Nov 24, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/Jim Urquhart)

Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a post on X that the operation was "a HUGE success."

"We are watching EPA's MASSIVE sensor array throughout the area closely, and there are no readings so far above 0.0," Telle said, referring to the Environmental Protection Agency.

EPA chief Lee Zeldin said on CNN that sampling showed there was "no detection" of lead for now.

The detonation of the explosives was initially scheduled for Nov 20 but was postponed for three days, after which Trump paused the operation pending a court decision and approval from the state's incoming governor, Rob Sand.

"EXTENSIVE PROTECTIVE WORKS"

The court cleared the way for the detonation in a ruling on Monday evening, while Sand said the same day that the "administration should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago".

Colonel Aaron Teller, who led the explosives experts who carried out the detonation, said the last major disposal of lead azide occurred in 1977, when some 7,000 pounds of the substance were destroyed in an open-air blast in Colorado.

Teller said in that case, 75 per cent of the lead particulate remained at the site even with no mitigation measures, and that steps were taken to better contain it in the Iowa detonation.

"There's extensive protective works around those two bunkers, earthen-filled barriers that extend well above the tops of those magazines," Teller told journalists ahead of the detonation.

There was also a vent in the protective works designed to send material released by the blast into an uninhabited area on the grounds of the ammunition plant.

Large water tanks were installed at the site to contain the explosion and keep lead particulate from entering the atmosphere, Teller said, while the Army also sought to curb the blast and the material it released by flooding the exterior of the magazines with a foam material.

Army personnel and local emergency management check in with residents in Middletown, Iowa, US, Nov 25, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/Jim Urquhart)

The Army released two maps on Wednesday, one showing potential exposure to toxic lead dust in the air in an area extending more than 75 miles (120km) southwest of the blast site, and another picturing possible exposure on surfaces in a more limited area.

"Consider avoiding the highlighted area or remain indoors with windows/doors closed," the maps said, warning that "children under six are especially vulnerable to lead exposure".

The Army also urged a local evacuation prior to the detonation, saying the Federal Emergency Management Agency was "supporting the recommended relocation for all residents of Middletown, Iowa, and immediate surrounding impacted areas".

"Evacuated individuals will be notified by phone once the all-clear is given and at that point may return home," the Army said.

items.title: Trump's accounts traded Nvidia shares 44 times this year, records show
items.summary: A review of the US president's financial disclosures shows Donald Trump's investment portfolios have regularly traded shares in the tech giant.
items.body:
Image source, Reuters

ByThomas Copeland and Alison Benjamin, BBC Verify

Donald Trump's investment portfolios have bought or sold shares in chipmaker Nvidia at least 44 times this year, a review of the US president's financial disclosures shows.

Trump's most recent public declarations of his investment trading show that between January and September the portfolios purchased between $5.2m and $17m (£4m and £13m) in Nvidia stock - and sold between $4.4m and $12m. His portfolios held between $12.5m and $58m of Nvidia shares at the end of 2025.

items.title: Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation
items.summary: As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their democratic processes?
items.body:

Nigeria's 2027 general election will take place against the backdrop of AI-driven disinformationImage: Adekunle Ajayi/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Advertisement

Nigeria has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis. He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi.

The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).

Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.

The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general election. Instead of making the upcoming vote more transparent by allowing access to its procedures, INEC has come under fire amid broader controversies about the expanding influence of AI in elections across the continent.

Is Nigeria becoming a one-party state?

Fake news: Nothing new in Nigeria

Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the electoral commission, said the body is now investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI use.

To this end, he announced the establishment of a dedicated unit to monitor AI-related threats, detect deepfakes and strengthen the integrity of the electoral process, warning that the credibility of the upcoming election could otherwise be under attack.

Supporters of a particular candidate in the election can be easily manipulated to believe AI-driven fake newsImage: Sani Maikatanga/AP Photo/picture alliance

However, even prior to the proliferation of AI across Africa and the globe, this would not be the first time that Nigeria has found itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the circulation of fabricated images, doctored audio and fake videos online. In the run-up to the 2023 election, deepfakes falsely linking candidates to terror-related activities filled social media platforms.

These are often designed to promote certain candidates or to discredit opponents in a bid to influence public perception, which now with the use of AI could create disinformation campaigns of new proportions.

Artificial intelligence has various effects on voter behavior

Lois Ugbede, the assistant editor at the factchecking platform DUBAWA, told DW that "based on our monitoring so far, AI-driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace."

"This could influence political discourse and voter behavior ahead of 2027 because we are already seeing parties using inflated crowds to show that they have a large followership or support," she added.

Have some elections become an empty ritual?

At the same time, rather than influencing the vote in favor of any particular candidate, "the deeper danger is that people may begin to doubt authentic information simply because they know convincing AI-generated fakes are possible," said Akintunde Babatunde, executive director of the Abuja-based Centre for Journalism, Innovation and Development.

"We often focus on the risk of people believing an AI-generated falsehood, but there is another problem where genuine evidence can be dismissed as AI-generated," he noted, citing instances of a lawmaker who recently made inflammatory remarks during a campaign rally — but then claimed the clips were manipulated.

Further pitfalls behind a lack of safeguards against AI

Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, an election consultant at the Centre for Democracy and Development, told DW that apart from the spread of synthetic content online, AI intrusion into the electoral commission's portal could also "undermine its institutional credibility, especially with the low level of confidence that we are already witnessing."

He added, however, that AI itself is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity. The real threat lies in "the absence of effective accountability for its deployment," as innovations in tech increasingly appear to infiltrate governments and their democratic processes.

"Voters must have confidence … that the technology is also transparent, accountable and independently scrutinized, and ultimately subject to human and institutional oversight," said Mgbeahuruike.

Journalists can be just as susceptible to disinformation created by AI and other technologiesImage: Emmanuel Osodi/AA/picture alliance

Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, the director-general of state-owned broadcaster Voice of Nigeria, agrees, urging journalists at a recent conference also to not fall into the trap of believing reports, which later could turn out to be false due to AI manipulation.

He stressed the importance of protection measures and due diligence in news media, with the growing inability of public institutions like INEC to provide impartial information due to the use and influence of AI and other election-related tech.

Nigeria's marred relationship with new tech

Beyond AI, Nigeria's electoral processes have undergone various technological shifts over the years in hopes of improving transparency while increasing efficiency.

Electoral authorities first deployed electronic assistance in 2011, when Direct Data Capture Machines were introduced; the devices collect voters' biometrics by scanning fingerprints or capturing facial recognition data with webcams to stop voters from submitting multiple ballots.

Ten years later, a system called the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced as the new standard, designed to combine fingerprints with facial recognition. However, during the 2023 general election, this voting process was marred by system failures, as poor cell signals delayed these voter accreditation procedures.

Nigeria's voting procedures have increasingly been digitalized since 2011Image: Pius Utomi Ekpei/AFP

However, with INEC tallying more than 103 million Nigerians registered to participate in the coming poll, disinformation, fake news and technological challenges amount to only a few of several concerns pertaining to Nigeria's democracy.

Voter apathy has become a particular concern, especially among the country's youth. The 2023 election recorded the lowest voter turnout since the country's return to democratic rule in 1999, with merely 27% of registered voters going to the polls.

items.title: Five Russian military jets hit in airfield strike, says Ukraine
items.summary: The Savasleyka airfield hosts aircraft used by Russia to launch hypersonic missiles and glide bombs at Ukraine.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

A Russian MiG-31 military jet (file photo)

ByLaura Gozzi

Ukraine has said it damaged five Russian military aircraft in an attack on Russia's Savasleyka airfield, 300km (185 miles) east of Moscow.

Three MiG-31 and two Su-34s aircraft were hit, Kyiv's General Staff said, adding that the extent of the damage was still being assessed but that "there may be even better news to come". It did not elaborate on what weapons it had used to hit the airfield.

Russia has not commented on the strikes.

The airfield at Savasleyka, in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, has been a target for Ukraine for several years. It hosts aircraft used by Russia to launch hypersonic missiles and glide bombs.

The take-off of MiG-31s in particular frequently triggers nationwide alerts across Ukraine, as the Kinzhal missiles they carry have been known to hit large infrastructure and military targets and are difficult to shoot down.

Overnight, Kyiv also said it hit two oil refineries in Russia's Samara region some 800km (500 miles) from the front line – the latest in a series of long-range strikes which have dented Moscow's oil processing capacity.

"Did you repair them? We'll hit them again," the defence ministry in Kyiv said.

Samara region governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said the night-time attacks had been "a true ordeal", with more than 145 drones shot down. One person was killed and several towns experienced power outages, Fedorishchev said.

Kyiv also said it had hit a radar system as well as fuel and logistics depots across Ukrainian territories currently occupied by Russia.

"Without fuel, military vehicles cannot move; without ammunition, artillery falls silent," the defence ministry said, adding that every successful hit meant Moscow could carry out fewer strikes.

Kyiv has developed a thriving weapons industry and Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets well beyond the front line have become commonplace in the years since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion.

On Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin called for a tightening of security measures across the country's energy facilities.

But he also argued that Russia had managed to stabilise its domestic fuel market without suffering "critical damage" and added that Moscow would "inevitably" retaliate against Kyiv.

Ukraine continues to come under daily attack. Ten people were killed across several regions between 24 and 25 November, while thousands are without power after Russian strikes on energy infrastructure.

items.title: How American Thanksgiving took root -- and evolved -- in Liberia
items.summary: The first settlers of Liberia were African Americans who brought along the holiday of Thanksgiving — which has evolved to reflect the history and identity of this new nation.
items.body:
Global Health

How American Thanksgiving took root — and evolved — in Liberia

November 25, 20269:14 AM ET

Ari Daniel

Yvonne Capehart Weah's family routinely gets together in the township where she grew up in Liberia. In early November every year, they gather to celebrate the Liberian version of Thanksgiving.

Eddie Raynes

hide caption

Eddie Raynes

Yvonne Capehart Weah is from Liberia, a country in West Africa, and she's one of twelve siblings.

"I'm the second to the last one — I'm the eleventh," she says. "We have large families in Liberia."

Every year on the first Thursday in November, Weah's family gathers in Caldwell, the township where she grew up, to celebrate Liberian Thanksgiving.

"When we come together, the group become [so] large that you are not able to sit around a dining table," she explains. "So we do it outside under the tree. And when we meet, it's almost like we're having a party."

The Liberian holiday dates back to the first half of the 19th century when the American Colonization Society established the community that would grow into the country. It was founded by Black Americans — both those born free and enslaved people who had been emancipated — whose departure was sometimes voluntary, sometimes forced. "The settlers from America brought that Thanksgiving Day tradition to Liberia," says Weah. Once transplanted, the holiday evolved over time in response to national events.

Liberia gained its independence in 1847 but the British continued trying to take swaths of territory. In 1883, President Alfred Francis Russell, an Episcopalian priest, called upon God to help halt the incursions.

That invocation was a "prayer of protection against the intruders, preventing intrusion into our territory," says Weah.

The Liberians managed to maintain their sovereignty. And that year, the legislature officially established Thanksgiving as a national holiday steeped in the religious gratitude of the moment.

A sacred day for all

Weah summarizes Liberian Thanksgiving this way: "It's giving thanks to God for our freedom, for divine protection. It's giving thanks to God for unity and for the harvest."

Weah says that her family's celebration, like that of many others in Liberia, starts in the morning at church. But the holiday's for people of all faiths, and other religious communities mark the occasion as well

"The Muslims, they go to the mosques and pray," says Sekou Muhammad Sheriff, a YouTuber who travels his home country of Liberia to showcase its offerings and cultural heritage, including Thanksgiving. "And Muslims, Christians, and others — everybody observe this day as a holiday."

When Sheriff was a boy, this was the day that he counted on to get a new outfit.

"What my dad used to do for me," says Sheriff, was to purchase a "shirt-trouser suit, and then he'd buy me slipper." His favorite suit was a white one.

Over the years on Thanksgiving, he's grown accustomed to eating different stews, including one made with sweet potato leaves and another with snails collected from the garden.

"We call it king's meat," Sheriff says with a chuckle. "It is very, very nice."

The mid-afternoon meal varies from household to household in Liberia.

Yvonne Capehart Weah's nieces and nephews fill their plates at a family gathering in Caldwell.

Rebecca Blapoh Weah

hide caption

Rebecca Blapoh Weah

"We don't do turkey," says Weah, "but we do chicken. We do fried chicken, smoked chicken, roasted chicken."

Weah's family also serves jollof rice, watermelon, pineapple and a variety of stews, including one called fufu and soup. It's a mix of cassava, fish, chicken, okra, chili pepper and more. "That makes the soup very tasty," says Weah. "It has to be [at] every Thanksgiving."

(Weah doesn't especially like to cook, however. "If you tell me, 'Go in the kitchen to cook or sit in the living room and read,'" she says, "I will sit in the living room and read.")

"I'm thanking God"

This year, Sheriff didn't have the resources to host Thanksgiving. But he says that he remains thankful to God for keeping him healthy and for keeping Liberia peaceful after civil conflict tore his country apart from 1989 to 1997 and 1999 to 2003.

Weah is also grateful. "When I go for Thanksgiving," she says, "I'm thanking God for where I have come from, where I am now, and I'm also thanking Him for where He will take me because I know He holds the future."

Weah is the program manager at the We-Care Foundation, an education nonprofit that, among other things, teaches children literacy. "A reading child will become a reading elder," she says.

"And we expect informed adults to make informed decisions that affect both their social and economic life" — in ways, perhaps, that they will one day be thankful for.
